analysis.one_liner: Requires the IRS to provide free online tax filing software and prepare simple returns itself.
analysis.headline: The bill won no action after its introduction: referred to the Ways and Means Committee in April 2019, it never received a markup or floor vote and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the IRS to build and run free online tax preparation and filing software for every taxpayer, let people download the income data the government already holds so it can pre-fill their returns, and prepare returns automatically for people with simple tax situations (single, standard deduction, wages, interest, and dividends only). It also would have barred the Treasury Secretary from signing any agreement that limits the IRS's right to offer these services, moved the deadline for employers and banks to send wage and interest data to January 31 so returns could be pre-filled earlier, and prohibited any fee for using the programs. It never received a committee vote or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Tens of millions of ordinary taxpayers, especially the roughly two-thirds who take the standard deduction and have simple situations: they could file for free in minutes using data the IRS already has, instead of paying for commercial software or a preparer. States that want to offer their own free filing programs would get federal data and technical help.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary taxpayers who file simple returns

how_it_helps.text: Requires the IRS to operate free online tax preparation and filing software, at no fee to any taxpayer who uses it, by January 31, 2021 [S2][S3].

Creates a program letting taxpayers download the third-party-reported information (wages, interest, dividends) the government already collects, in computer-readable form suitable for automated preparation, within 15 days of the IRS receiving it [S3].

Lets eligible individuals — initially single filers with no business income who claim the standard deduction and have only wages, interest, and dividends — elect to have the IRS prepare their return for them, with eligibility expandable afterward at the Secretary's discretion [S3].
Moves the deadline for information returns (W-2s, 1099s) to January 31 with no extensions, so taxpayers get the data they need earlier in filing season [S3].

Prohibits the Treasury Secretary from entering any agreement that restricts the IRS's legal right to provide tax preparation or filing services — closing off arrangements of the kind the IRS had with private tax prep companies, whose 'Free File' program limits the government's own role [S3][S2].
Provides federal data and technical assistance to states that offer or plan to offer their own free state-level filing programs [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Commercial tax preparation and software companies (such as Intuit's TurboTax and H&R Block) would lose customers and revenue, particularly among simple-return filers. Paid preparers and tax software workers would face reduced demand. The IRS would bear the cost of building and running the programs, funded by appropriations authorized for fiscal years 2020 through 2024, and credit reporting agencies would lose a channel for identity-verification services.
analysis.who_pays_short: Tax prep software companies and paid preparers

drawbacks.text: Building and running federal filing software costs taxpayer money; the bill authorizes appropriations of such sums as necessary for fiscal years 2020 through 2024 [S3].

The initial eligibility for IRS-prepared returns is narrow — single filers, standard deduction, wages/interest/dividends only — so in its first years the automatic-preparation program would reach a minority of taxpayers, with expansion left to the Secretary's discretion [S3].

The bill bans knowledge-based identity verification, including procedures supplied through credit reporting agencies, a rule adopted after IRS data breaches raised fraud concerns but one that could make secure access harder for some taxpayers to set up [S3].

Nothing in the bill absolves taxpayers of responsibility for the accuracy of their return, so people using IRS-prepared returns would still be on the hook for errors if the underlying data was incomplete [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete and large for most filers: free, fast filing using data the government already has, ending a system where taxpayers pay companies to do arithmetic on numbers the IRS already receives. The main costs are the IRS build-out expense and the disruption to the private tax prep industry, which is the point of the bill rather than an accident. The narrow initial eligibility for fully automatic IRS preparation is a real limitation, though the free software program would be open to everyone.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up; it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Sherman introduced the Tax Filing Simplification Act of 2019 on April 12, 2019, joined by eight original cosponsors [S1][S3].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means — the committee that handles tax legislation [S1][S5].
No further action was ever recorded: no hearing, no markup, no vote, and no floor consideration through the end of the Congress [S5].

The bill's core provision — barring agreements that restrict the IRS from offering its own filing services — targets the existing arrangement between the IRS and private tax software companies, under which the government agrees to stay out of tax preparation in exchange for companies offering limited free filing [S3][S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The commercial tax preparation and software industry is better off: no competitor emerged from the IRS, and the existing market for paid filing software and preparers was left intact.

for.name: Rep. Brad Sherman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require the IRS to offer free filing and prepare simple returns

against.name: Rep. Richard Neal
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or hearing on the bill, leaving it without any committee action for the rest of the Congress

against.name: Tax preparation software industry (Intuit, H&R Block)
against.role: Commercial tax filing software and preparation companies
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against government-run free tax filing and defended the private Free File arrangement the bill sought to prohibit

sides.party_line_note: All ten supporters — the sponsor and nine cosponsors — were Democrats, and no Republican signed on.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and filing software companies (Intuit, H&R Block)
industries.note: The bill creates a free government competitor and, more pointedly, bars the IRS from signing agreements that limit its own right to provide these services — threatening the market position these companies have built, including through the Free File arrangement with the IRS. Ordinary people pay these companies to file returns the government could largely pre-fill for free, so the industry's interest runs against filers here.

industries.industry: Paid tax preparers and tax software workers
industries.note: Simple-return filers would shift to free government software and IRS preparation, reducing demand for paid preparation of straightforward returns. Complex-return work would remain.
The bill bans identity verification through knowledge-based procedures supplied via credit reporting agencies, cutting off a service channel those agencies provide to the IRS.

industries.industry: State revenue agencies offering free filing
industries.note: States that provide or plan to provide free state-level filing software would receive federal tax data and technical assistance, making their programs easier to launch.
